title: Book VIII: Sunset And Sunrise — Chapter LXXII
paragraphs:
Full souls are facing mirrors, stretching out
An endless view of lovely things ahead,
Reflecting what lies behind.

Dorothea’s impulsive generosity would have rushed to defend Lydgate against the suspicion that he had accepted a bribe. But as she considered the whole case in the light of Mr. Farebrother’s experience, her confidence met a discouraging check.

“It’s a delicate subject to raise,” he said. “How could we investigate? Either publicly, by involving the magistrate and coroner, or privately, by questioning Lydgate. There’s no firm basis for the first course, or Hawley would have taken it. As for speaking to Lydgate, I admit I’d hesitate. He would probably consider it a grave insult. I’ve found it difficult more than once to talk to him about personal matters. And to feel confident of a good outcome, we would need to know the truth about his conduct already.”

“I’m convinced he has done nothing wrong. I believe people are almost always better than their neighbors think,” Dorothea said. Some of her most intense experiences over the previous two years had turned her firmly against putting the worst interpretation on others’ actions. For the first time, she felt a little dissatisfied with Farebrother. She disliked this cautious calculation of consequences. She wanted passionate faith in justice and mercy, whose very emotional force could make them prevail. Two days later he dined at the Manor with her uncle and the Chettams. With dessert still untouched, the servants out of the room, and Mr. Brooke nodding in sleep, she returned to the subject with fresh energy.

“Mr. Lydgate would understand that when his friends hear a slander, their first wish is to clear his name. What are we alive for, if not to make life easier for one another? I can’t stand aside when a man is in trouble who advised me in _my_ trouble and cared for me when I was ill.”

Dorothea spoke and acted no more forcefully than she had at the head of her uncle’s table nearly three years earlier. The experience she had gained since gave her a stronger right to a definite opinion. But Sir James Chettam was no longer a shy, agreeable suitor. He was an anxious brother-in-law, devoted in his admiration of her, yet constantly afraid she would fall into another delusion almost as bad as marrying Casaubon. He smiled much less. His “Exactly” now more often introduced a disagreement than it had in his submissive bachelor days. Dorothea was surprised to find she had to make up her mind not to fear him, especially because he really was her best friend. Now he disagreed.
“But, Dorothea,” he protested, “you can’t take charge of a man’s life like that. Lydgate must know—or soon will know—where he stands. If he can clear himself, he will. He must act on his own behalf.”

“I think his friends must wait for an opportunity,” Farebrother added. “It is possible—I’ve felt so much weakness in myself that I can imagine even an honorable man, as I’ve always considered Lydgate, yielding to a temptation like this: accepting money offered, more or less indirectly, to buy his silence about old scandals. I can imagine it if he were under severe pressure, troubled as I’m sure Lydgate has been. I wouldn’t believe anything worse without strong proof. But some errors carry a terrible punishment: anyone who chooses can interpret them as crimes. The man has nothing to prove otherwise except his own knowledge of himself and his word.”

“How cruel!” Dorothea cried, clasping her hands. “Wouldn’t you want to be the one person who believed him innocent when everyone else spoke falsely against him? Besides, his earlier character speaks for him.”

“But, my dear Mrs. Casaubon,” Farebrother said, smiling gently at her fervor, “character isn’t carved in marble. It isn’t fixed and unchangeable. It lives and changes, and it can grow sick just as our bodies do.”

“Then it can be saved and healed,” Dorothea answered. “I wouldn’t be afraid to ask Mr. Lydgate for the truth so I could help him. Why should I be afraid? Since I’m not to have the land, James, I could do what Mr. Bulstrode suggested and take over his support of the hospital. I must consult Mr. Lydgate to understand what good we can hope to do by keeping the present plans. That gives me the best possible opportunity to ask for his confidence. He could tell me things that explain everything. Then we could all stand by him and bring him through his trouble. People praise every kind of courage except the courage they could show for their own neighbors.” Her eyes shone with moisture. The change in her voice woke her uncle, who began listening.
“It’s true that a woman may attempt some expressions of sympathy that would scarcely succeed if a man tried them,” said Farebrother, almost persuaded by her intensity.

“Surely a woman ought to be cautious and listen to people who know more of the world,” Sir James said with his small frown. “Whatever you eventually do, Dorothea, you really should hold back for now and not volunteer to interfere in this Bulstrode affair. We don’t yet know what might emerge. You must agree?” he concluded, turning to Farebrother.
“I do think waiting would be wiser,” Farebrother replied.

“Yes, yes, my dear,” Brooke put in. He did not quite know where the discussion had got to, but offered something generally applicable. “It’s easy to go too far, you know. Don’t let your ideas carry you away. And rushing to put money into schemes—that won’t do. Garth has got me spending remarkably heavily on repairs, drainage, that sort of thing. One thing after another, and I’m very much out of pocket. I must rein it in. And you, Chettam, you’re spending a fortune on those oak fences round your estate.”
Submitting unhappily to this discouragement, Dorothea went with Celia into the library, which she generally used as a drawing room.

“Now, Dodo, do listen to James,” Celia said. “Otherwise you’ll get yourself into trouble. You always did, and you always will, when you insist on pleasing yourself. After everything, I think it’s a blessing you have James to think for you. He lets you keep your plans, only he stops people taking advantage of you. That’s the good of having a brother instead of a husband. A husband wouldn’t let you keep your plans.”
“As though I wanted a husband!” Dorothea said. “I only want my feelings to stop being checked at every turn.” Mrs. Casaubon had still not mastered herself enough to prevent angry tears.

“Really, Dodo,” said Celia, her voice a little more throaty than usual, “you _are_ contradictory. First one thing, then another. You used to give in to Mr. Casaubon quite shamefully. I believe you’d have stopped visiting me altogether if he’d asked.”
“Of course I gave in to him. It was my duty. It came from my feeling for him,” Dorothea said, looking through the prism of her tears.

“Then why can’t you think it your duty to give in a little to James?” Celia asked, feeling the force of her argument. “He only wants what’s best for you. And of course men know best about everything except the things women know better.” Dorothea laughed and forgot to cry.
“Well, I mean babies and things like that,” Celia explained. “I wouldn’t give in to James when I knew he was wrong, the way you did with Mr. Casaubon.”
